central_ideas.p: Lighthouses once needed keepers who lived on site and tended the lamps every night. Today, nearly all lighthouses run automatically. Sensors switch the lights on at dusk, and technicians visit only for repairs.
central_ideas.r: Lighthouses that once required keepers now mostly operate on their own.
w: Lighthouse keepers enjoyed living near the sea.
Technicians visit lighthouses every night.
Most lighthouses have been torn down.
central_ideas.e: The text contrasts past keepers with today’s automatic lights. The other choices add details or contradict “only for repairs.”

central_ideas.p: Mina’s grandmother taught her to fold dumplings when Mina was six. At first her dumplings fell apart in the pot. After many tries, she learned to pinch the edges tightly. Now she teaches her younger cousins the same way.
central_ideas.r: Mina learned a skill through practice and now passes it on.
w: Mina does not enjoy cooking with her family.
Mina’s grandmother refuses to teach her cousins.
Mina’s dumplings always fall apart in the pot.
central_ideas.e: The text moves from her first failures to skill to teaching others. Her dumplings fell apart only “at first.”

central_ideas.p: Plants in a city can do more than look nice. Trees shade streets and buildings, which lowers summer temperatures. Their leaves trap dust, and their roots absorb rainwater that might otherwise flood roads.
central_ideas.r: City plants provide several practical benefits.
w: City trees are difficult to keep alive.
Flooding is the worst problem in most cities.
Plants in cities are mainly decorative.
central_ideas.e: The text lists cooling, cleaner air, and flood control as benefits. It says plants do “more than look nice,” which contradicts “mainly decorative.”

central_ideas.p: The Great Wall of China is not one continuous wall. It is a series of walls and forts built by different dynasties over about two thousand years. Some sections are made of stone or brick, while others are packed earth.
central_ideas.r: The Great Wall is really many structures built at different times.
w: The Great Wall was finished in a single dynasty.
Stone is the only material used in the Great Wall.
The forts along the wall are older than the walls.
central_ideas.e: The main point is that it isn’t one wall but many sections built over time. Each wrong choice contradicts a detail or adds one that isn’t there.

central_ideas.p: When ecologists reintroduced beavers to a stretch of river in Scotland, they expected changes in the water but not on the scale that followed. The dams slowed the current and created ponds that held back floodwater after heavy rain. Dragonflies, frogs, and water birds moved into the new wetlands within a few seasons, and water leaving the area was noticeably cleaner than water arriving.
central_ideas.r: Returning beavers to the river reshaped the area in ways that benefited both water and wildlife.
w: Beaver dams cause more flooding after heavy rain than natural rivers do.
Scottish ecologists were disappointed by how slowly the wetlands appeared.
Dragonflies and frogs are the species most dependent on beaver dams.
central_ideas.e: The text lists flood control, new wildlife, and cleaner water, all from the beavers’ return. Dams reduced flooding, and no ranking of species is offered.

central_ideas.p:
The following text is adapted from a novel. Lena has returned to her childhood town after many years.

The bakery had a new sign, and the old oak by the school was gone, but what unsettled Lena most was how small everything looked. The hill she had once dreaded on her bicycle was hardly a slope. She stood at the bottom of it for some time, trying to feel the size of what she remembered.
central_ideas.r: Lena is struck by how different the town seems from her memories of it.
w: Lena regrets having left her town at a young age.
Lena is angry that the old oak has been cut down.
Lena plans to ride her bicycle up the hill again.
central_ideas.e: The passage focuses on the gap between memory and reality: “how small everything looked.” Regret, anger, and plans go beyond what’s stated.

central_ideas.p: Most museums display only a small fraction of what they own; the rest sits in storage. A growing number of institutions are responding by building “visible storage,” in which shelves of objects can be seen through glass by anyone who walks by. Curators say these spaces reveal how collections are actually organized and invite visitors to find objects no exhibit would have chosen for them.
central_ideas.r: Some museums are making stored objects viewable, which offers visitors a new way of experiencing collections.
w: Museums have run out of space because they own too many objects.
Curators believe exhibits should no longer select objects for display.
Glass storage protects objects better than traditional storage rooms.
central_ideas.e: The text is about visible storage and what it offers visitors. It doesn’t say exhibits should end or compare protection.

central_ideas.p: Sleep researchers once treated dreaming as a by-product of random brain activity. Later studies complicated that view. People who practiced a new task and then dreamed about it improved more on the task the next day than those who practiced but didn’t dream about it. Researchers caution that the link isn’t fully understood, but such results suggest that dreaming may play some role in learning.
central_ideas.r: Evidence suggests dreaming may contribute to learning, though the connection remains uncertain.
w: Dreaming has been proven to be the main way people learn new tasks.
Random brain activity is unrelated to the sleeping brain.
People who dream less have more difficulty sleeping at night.
central_ideas.e: “May play some role” and “isn’t fully understood” call for a cautious statement. “Proven” and “the main way” are far too strong.

central_ideas.p: The notion that Renaissance painters abruptly discovered perspective through mathematics has given way to a more gradual account. Workshop records show that artists experimented for decades with practical devices, including grids and mirrors, well before any theory was written down. Treatises such as Alberti’s, on this view, did less to invent a new technique than to organize and lend intellectual prestige to methods already circulating among craftsmen.
central_ideas.r: Perspective developed through artists’ practical experimentation, with written theory later codifying it rather than creating it.
w: Alberti’s treatise was largely ignored by the craftsmen of his own time.
Renaissance painters rejected mathematics in favor of mirrors and grids.
Written theories of perspective led directly to the workshop experiments.
central_ideas.e: The point is that practice came first and treatises organized it. The last choice reverses the order, and the text never says painters rejected math or that Alberti was ignored.

central_ideas.p:
The following text is adapted from an essay on the novelist George Eliot.

Eliot’s narrators seldom let a character’s failing pass without comment, and readers might expect such attention to harden into judgment. It doesn’t. Her habit is to follow the most self-deceiving character into the private reasoning that made the error seem sensible, so that condemnation becomes difficult. The reader who begins by feeling superior to a vain clergyman finishes by recognizing how ordinary his vanity is, and how close to one’s own.
central_ideas.r: Eliot’s close attention to characters’ flaws leads readers toward understanding rather than condemnation.
w: Eliot’s narrators refuse to comment on the moral failings of their characters.
Eliot’s novels mainly criticize the clergymen of her time.
Eliot’s characters come to recognize their errors by the end of each novel.
central_ideas.e: The essay says her attention doesn’t “harden into judgment” and leads to recognition. Narrators do comment, and it’s the reader, not the character, who recognizes something.

central_ideas.p: Public discussions of recycling often assume that the chief obstacle is consumer behavior: if people sorted more carefully, more material would be reused. Yet studies of municipal systems point elsewhere. Much of what residents place in bins cannot be profitably processed, because the market for recovered plastics fluctuates with the price of oil, and new plastic is frequently cheaper than reclaimed material. Even perfectly sorted waste, in other words, may end up in a landfill when no one will pay to take it.
central_ideas.r: Recycling outcomes depend heavily on economic conditions, not just on how well consumers sort their waste.
w: Consumers are sorting their waste more carefully than they did in the past.
Plastic should be replaced by other materials that are more easily recycled.
Municipal recycling systems are unnecessary because most waste ends up in landfills.
central_ideas.e: The text shifts attention from sorting to markets and prices. It makes no claim about trends in sorting, replacing plastic, or ending recycling programs.

central_ideas.p: Early accounts of the Dust Bowl presented it as a natural disaster, a drought of unusual severity striking the Great Plains in the 1930s. Later historians have argued that this framing obscures human choices. Decades of plowing had stripped away the deep-rooted grasses that once anchored the soil, and federal land policy, along with high wheat prices, had encouraged that expansion. The drought was real, these historians grant, but it became catastrophic only on land already made vulnerable.
central_ideas.r: The Dust Bowl resulted from the interaction of drought with earlier farming practices and policies.
w: The drought of the 1930s was less severe than early accounts claimed.
High wheat prices were the main reason that the drought occurred.
Farmers on the Great Plains opposed federal land policy in the 1930s.
central_ideas.e: “The drought was real... but it became catastrophic only on land already made vulnerable” shows both causes working together. The text doesn’t question its severity, and prices didn’t cause the drought.

evidence_textual.s: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates this claim?
evidence_textual.p: In a poem by Rosa Lind, the speaker views the sea as peaceful.
evidence_textual.r: “The waves breathe softly on the sand, / a slow and quiet tune.”
w: “The storm tears ships apart at night / and howls along the shore.”
“I left my village long ago / and never sailed again.”
“The market fills with fish and salt, / and shouting fills the air.”
evidence_textual.e: Soft breathing and a quiet tune show a peaceful sea. The storm is violent, and the other two aren’t about the sea’s calm.

evidence_textual.s: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the coach’s claim?
evidence_textual.p: A high school track coach claims that students who get at least eight hours of sleep run faster in practice than students who get less sleep.
evidence_textual.r: Runners who slept eight or more hours had faster practice times than those who slept less.
w: Runners who ate breakfast were more likely to attend practice.
Most students at the school do not get eight hours of sleep.
Practice times were faster on cool days than on hot days.
evidence_textual.e: Only this finding links sleep amount to running speed. The other choices involve breakfast, general habits, or weather.

evidence_textual.s: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the hypothesis?
evidence_textual.p: A student hypothesizes that tomato plants grown with music will grow taller than tomato plants grown in silence.
evidence_textual.r: Tomato plants in a room with music grew taller than plants in a quiet room.
w: Tomato plants grew taller with more sunlight.
Students enjoyed playing music in the greenhouse.
Tomato plants in the quiet room produced the same amount of fruit.
evidence_textual.e: The hypothesis compares height with and without music, so that comparison is the direct support.

evidence_textual.s: Which quotation from the letter most effectively illustrates the claim?
evidence_textual.p: In a letter, the nineteenth-century traveler Clara Wells shows how tired she has grown of her long journey by stagecoach.
evidence_textual.r: “I have counted every mile, and I would give a year of my life to sleep in a still bed.”
w: “The mountains here are the finest I have ever seen.”
“My sister writes that the harvest was good this year.”
“We shall reach the river by Tuesday, the driver says.”
evidence_textual.e: Counting miles and longing for a still bed show weariness. The others are simple observations or news.

evidence_textual.s: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Tanaka’s hypothesis?
evidence_textual.p: Some songbirds sing at a higher pitch in cities than in the countryside. Biologist Hana Tanaka hypothesizes that this is because low-pitched traffic noise drowns out lower notes, so birds that sing higher are heard more easily by mates and rivals.
evidence_textual.r: Within the same city, birds of a given species sing at a higher pitch near busy roads than in quiet parks.
w: Birds in cities begin singing earlier in the morning than birds in the countryside.
Traffic noise in cities has increased steadily over the past fifty years.
Birds that live in the countryside tend to have larger territories than city birds.
evidence_textual.e: Tying pitch directly to noise levels, in the same city, tests her explanation. Timing, noise trends alone, and territory size don’t link noise to pitch.

evidence_textual.s: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the researchers’ claim?
evidence_textual.p: Researchers studying a small island’s forest claim that the decline of a native fruit-eating bird has reduced the spread of a certain tree, since the bird was the main animal that carried the tree’s seeds to new sites.
evidence_textual.r: Young trees of that species are appearing at new sites at the same rate as before the bird declined.
w: The bird’s decline began shortly after a new predator arrived on the island.
Several other tree species on the island also produce fruit eaten by the bird.
The tree’s fruit ripens during the season when the bird is most active.
evidence_textual.e: If the tree keeps spreading at the same rate, the bird’s decline hasn’t reduced it. The other findings don’t bear on whether seed spread has fallen.

evidence_textual.s: Which quotation from the novel most effectively illustrates the claim?
evidence_textual.p: In a 1920s novel by Adele Marsh, the narrator suggests that the character Mr. Hollis cares more about how he appears to others than about the truth.
evidence_textual.r: “Hollis would rather be admired for a falsehood than go unnoticed for an honest remark.”
w: “Hollis walked each morning to the post office, whatever the weather.”
“Hollis had inherited the house from an uncle he barely knew.”
“Hollis spoke rarely, and when he did it was usually about his garden.”
evidence_textual.e: This line directly compares admiration with honesty. The others are neutral details about his habits and history.

evidence_textual.s: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the claim?
evidence_textual.p: A team of nutrition researchers argues that a town’s new farmers’ market, rather than a general trend, was responsible for the increase in fruit and vegetable purchases among the town’s residents after the market opened in 2021.
evidence_textual.r: Purchases rose in the town after 2021 but stayed flat in similar nearby towns without new markets.
w: Fruit and vegetable prices at the market were similar to those at local supermarkets.
Residents reported that they enjoyed the live music played at the market.
The market was located near the town’s largest public park.
evidence_textual.e: Comparing with similar towns rules out a general trend, which is exactly what the claim needs. The other choices don’t address cause.

evidence_textual.s: Which finding, if true, would most directly undermine Okafor’s conclusion?
evidence_textual.p: Economist Ngozi Okafor studied a city that raised its minimum wage in 2016. Restaurant employment there grew over the next three years, and Okafor concluded that the increase did not reduce restaurant jobs. Critics note that the city’s population was growing rapidly over the same period, so restaurant jobs might have grown even without the wage increase, and perhaps faster.
evidence_textual.r: In comparable fast-growing cities with no wage increase, restaurant employment rose substantially more than it did in the city Okafor studied.
w: Restaurants in the city raised their menu prices slightly in the years after 2016.
Employment in the city’s other industries also increased between 2016 and 2019.
Workers in the city reported higher satisfaction with their jobs after the wage increase.
evidence_textual.e: If similar cities gained more jobs without the increase, the raise may have held employment back. Higher prices or other industries’ growth don’t show that restaurant jobs were reduced.

evidence_textual.s: Which quotation from the essay most effectively illustrates the claim?
evidence_textual.p: In an essay, the critic Helen Brandt argues that the value of a difficult book lies in the effort of reading it, and not merely in the ideas that a summary could convey.
evidence_textual.r: “What the slow reader carries away is not a set of conclusions, which any synopsis could supply, but a mind altered by the labor of arriving at them.”
w: “A summary may often be more accurate than the opinions of those who have read a book too quickly.”
“Few modern novels reward the attention of readers as generously as those of the last century.”
“The conclusions of a difficult book are usually simpler than its admirers are willing to admit.”
evidence_textual.e: This quotation names both parts of the claim: a synopsis gives conclusions, while the labor itself changes the reader. The others touch on summaries or difficulty but don’t say value lies in the effort.

evidence_textual.s: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ explanation?
evidence_textual.p: Fossil beds show that a group of large marine reptiles disappeared some 90 million years ago, a time of rapid warming and low oxygen in deep ocean water. Some researchers argue that the reptiles were not killed directly by these conditions. Instead, they propose, the low-oxygen water reduced the populations of deep-dwelling squid-like animals on which the reptiles depended, leaving them without enough to eat.
evidence_textual.r: Fossils of the reptiles’ deep-dwelling prey decline sharply in rock layers immediately below the layers in which the reptiles themselves vanish.
w: Other marine reptiles that fed near the surface vanished at the same moment as the deep-feeding group.
The reptiles’ bones show adaptations that would have let them tolerate warm water.
Ocean temperatures rose more quickly in that period than in any earlier period.
evidence_textual.e: Prey dropping first fits the food-chain explanation. Surface feeders vanishing at the same moment would point away from that explanation, and heat tolerance alone doesn’t show that prey loss was the cause.

evidence_textual.s: Which finding, if true, would most directly challenge the historian’s argument?
evidence_textual.p: A historian argues that the sharp rise in literacy in one European region between 1650 and 1750 resulted mainly from Protestant churches’ demand that members read scripture, rather than from economic growth in the region’s towns.
evidence_textual.r: Within the region, literacy rose as fast in Catholic towns with growing trade as in Protestant towns, and slowly in poorer Protestant villages.
w: Many of the region’s Protestant churches established schools during the period.
Literacy rates were higher among men than among women throughout the period.
Printing costs fell steadily across all of Europe between 1650 and 1750.
evidence_textual.e: This pattern tracks trade rather than religion, the opposite of the argument. Church schools would support it, and gender gaps don’t bear on the cause.

evidence_quantitative.s: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
evidence_quantitative.p:
Books Borrowed from the Oakdale Library
Month | Fiction | Nonfiction
June | 420 | 310
July | 510 | 290
August | 480 | 300

The librarian noticed that summer readers preferred fiction. In every month shown, ______
evidence_quantitative.r: more fiction books were borrowed than nonfiction books.
w: more nonfiction books were borrowed than fiction books.
the number of nonfiction books borrowed was above 400.
the number of fiction books borrowed decreased each month.
evidence_quantitative.e: Fiction is higher in June, July, and August. Nonfiction stays near 300, and fiction rose in July.

evidence_quantitative.s: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student’s claim?
evidence_quantitative.p:
Average Daily Temperature (°F) by City
City | January | July
Seattle | 42 | 66
Miami | 68 | 84
Denver | 32 | 75

A student claims that of the three cities, Denver has the largest temperature change between January and July.
evidence_quantitative.r: Denver’s temperature rises by 43 degrees, compared with 24 degrees in Seattle and 16 degrees in Miami.
w: Denver’s January temperature is 32 degrees, the lowest of the three cities.
Miami has the highest temperature in both January and July.
Seattle’s July temperature is 66 degrees, the lowest of the three cities.
evidence_quantitative.e: The claim is about the change, so the differences must be compared: 43, 24, and 16. The other choices give single temperatures.

evidence_quantitative.s: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researchers’ conclusion?
evidence_quantitative.p:
Pollinator Visits per Hour to Garden Plots
Plot type | Bees | Butterflies | Flies
Native flowers | 34 | 12 | 9
Ornamental flowers | 15 | 11 | 10
Mixed flowers | 26 | 12 | 9

Researchers concluded that planting native flowers particularly benefits bees, while it makes little difference for other pollinators.
evidence_quantitative.r: Bee visits were more than twice as frequent in native plots as in ornamental plots, while butterfly and fly visits were about the same across plot types.
w: Butterfly visits were highest in plots with native and mixed flowers, at 12 visits per hour.
Bees made more visits than butterflies and flies in every type of plot.
Mixed flower plots received 26 bee visits per hour and 9 fly visits per hour.
evidence_quantitative.e: The conclusion has two parts: a big gain for bees and little change for others. Only the correct choice addresses both. The others are true of the table but miss that comparison.

evidence_quantitative.s: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
evidence_quantitative.p:
Share of Trips Made by Bicycle (%)
City | 2010 | 2020
Amsel | 12 | 19
Brookton | 4 | 5
Corvale | 8 | 16

Cities that built protected bike lanes during the decade often saw large increases in cycling. Corvale, which built such lanes, offers an example: ______
evidence_quantitative.r: the share of trips made by bicycle there doubled from 8 percent to 16 percent.
w: its share of bicycle trips in 2020 was lower than Amsel’s share.
its share of bicycle trips was higher than Brookton’s in 2010.
the share of trips made by bicycle in Brookton rose by only 1 percentage point.
evidence_quantitative.e: A large increase in Corvale is the needed example, and doubling shows it. Comparisons with other cities at one moment don’t show an increase there.

evidence_quantitative.s: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to weaken the claim?
evidence_quantitative.p:
Survey of Adults Who Read at Least One Book in the Past Year (%)
Age group | 2012 | 2022
18–29 | 71 | 69
30–49 | 68 | 66
50–64 | 66 | 58
65+ | 63 | 52

A columnist claims that book reading is declining mainly because young adults spend their time on phones instead.
evidence_quantitative.r: The two oldest age groups had the largest declines, while reading among adults aged 18–29 fell by only 2 percentage points.
w: In both 2012 and 2022, adults aged 18–29 were the group most likely to have read a book.
Reading declined in every age group between 2012 and 2022.
More than half of adults in every age group had read a book in 2022.
evidence_quantitative.e: If the decline is mainly due to the young, they should show the biggest drop, but the oldest groups do. A decline in every group doesn’t separate who drives it.

evidence_quantitative.s: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
evidence_quantitative.p:
Effect of Two Fertilizers on Wheat Trial Plots
Treatment | Yield (tons per hectare) | Nitrogen lost to runoff (kg per hectare)
No fertilizer | 3.1 | 4
Fertilizer A | 5.2 | 31
Fertilizer B | 4.9 | 12

An agronomist argues that Fertilizer B is the better choice for farms near rivers, since ______
evidence_quantitative.r: it produced nearly the same yield as Fertilizer A while losing well under half as much nitrogen to runoff.
w: it produced a higher yield than the plots that received no fertilizer.
Fertilizer A produced the highest yield of the three treatments.
the plots that received no fertilizer lost the least nitrogen to runoff.
evidence_quantitative.e: Near rivers, runoff matters, and B must be compared with A on both yield and runoff: 4.9 versus 5.2 tons, 12 versus 31 kg. The other choices are true but don’t show B is better than A.

inferences.p: Ravi noticed that the plants on his sunny windowsill were growing quickly, while the same kind of plants on a dark shelf had stopped growing. He concluded that ______
inferences.r: the plants on the shelf needed more light.
w: the plants on the windowsill needed less water.
the shelf was too warm for any plant.
the plants on the windowsill were a different kind.
inferences.e: The only stated difference is light, and the plants are the same kind, so lack of light is the logical conclusion.

inferences.p: Every student who attended the review session on Tuesday passed the quiz. Julia failed the quiz. Therefore, Julia ______
inferences.r: did not attend the review session on Tuesday.
w: attended the review session on Tuesday.
studied more than the other students.
took the quiz on Wednesday.
inferences.e: All attendees passed, so anyone who failed cannot have attended.

inferences.p: Old maps of the village show a river running along Main Street. Today there is no river there, but the houses on Main Street still flood during storms, and water pipes must be placed unusually deep. This suggests that ______
inferences.r: the river may still be affecting the land beneath the street.
w: the old maps were drawn by people who had never seen the village.
the houses on Main Street were built before the village existed.
storms in the village have stopped in recent years.
inferences.e: Flooding and deep pipes along the old course point to the river’s continuing influence.

inferences.p: Squirrels bury far more nuts than they later dig up. Some of the forgotten nuts sprout in spring. As a result, squirrels ______
inferences.r: help new trees grow without intending to.
w: usually starve during the winter months.
eat only nuts that have already sprouted.
prevent oak forests from spreading.
inferences.e: Forgotten nuts sprout into trees, so the squirrels unintentionally plant them.

inferences.p: The ancient city of Ubar appears in many old stories, but for centuries no one could locate it. In the 1990s, satellite images revealed faint caravan tracks in the Arabian desert that all met at one point. Since the tracks seem to have been made by traders traveling to a common destination, researchers reasoned that ______
inferences.r: the meeting point of the tracks might mark the location of a major settlement.
w: the old stories about Ubar were invented by the traders themselves.
satellite images are more reliable than archaeological digging.
traders avoided settlements when crossing the desert.
inferences.e: Routes that converge on one point suggest a destination, likely a settlement. The other choices aren’t supported by the tracks.

inferences.p: In a study of a fishing community, researchers found that older fishers could predict weather changes with accuracy close to that of local forecasts, relying on cloud shapes and bird behavior. Younger fishers, who use phone apps, could not do the same when asked to rely on observation alone. These findings suggest that ______
inferences.r: reliance on technology may be reducing a kind of knowledge that was once common in the community.
w: phone apps are less accurate than the observations of older fishers.
younger fishers go out to sea less often than older fishers do.
birds change their behavior in response to local weather forecasts.
inferences.e: Older skill plus younger reliance on apps suggests the skill is fading. The study found observation was close to forecasts, not better than them.

inferences.p: A chemist testing a new battery material found that it stored more energy than current materials but lost its capacity after a few dozen charges. Because consumers expect phone batteries to last for hundreds of charges, the chemist concluded that ______
inferences.r: the material would need to become far more durable before it could be used in phones.
w: the material could immediately replace current phone batteries.
consumers would prefer phones that stored less energy.
phone batteries are charged less often than they once were.
inferences.e: A few dozen charges falls short of hundreds, so durability must improve before use.

inferences.p: Paintings by the Dutch artist Judith Leyster were sold for centuries under the name of her better-known contemporary Frans Hals. Only in 1893, when a dealer’s dispute led experts to examine one painting closely and find her monogram beneath a forged signature, did her work begin to be recognized. This episode suggests that ______
inferences.r: some artists’ reputations have been shaped by misattribution as well as by the quality of their work.
w: Leyster’s paintings were less skillful than those of Frans Hals.
art dealers in the 1800s were unwilling to sell Dutch paintings.
most Dutch paintings of the period carry forged signatures.
inferences.e: Her work went unrecognized because it was credited to Hals, showing that misattribution shaped her reputation. “Most” paintings overgeneralizes from one case.

inferences.p: Many species of deep-sea fish produce their own light, and for decades biologists assumed that this ability had evolved only a few times. A recent analysis of fish genomes, however, indicates that bioluminescence arose independently at least twenty-five times. Because a trait that appears repeatedly in unrelated lineages is likely to offer a substantial advantage in the conditions those lineages share, the analysis implies that ______
inferences.r: producing light is probably of considerable value to survival in the deep sea.
w: the earliest bioluminescent fish were the ancestors of all living deep-sea species.
fish living near the surface are unable to develop any form of bioluminescence.
the genes responsible for bioluminescence are identical in all light-producing fish.
inferences.e: The text’s general rule says repeated evolution implies an advantage in shared conditions, and these fish share the deep sea. Independent origins contradict a single ancestor and identical genes.

inferences.p: Medieval manuscripts sometimes contain marginal drawings of knights fighting giant snails, images that have puzzled scholars for generations. One proposal held that the snails symbolized a particular enemy of the Church, but the images appear in manuscripts from regions and decades in which that enemy played no role. Since a symbol tied to a specific historical group would not be expected to appear where that group was unknown, the proposal ______
inferences.r: seems unable to account for the full range of manuscripts in which the images appear.
w: correctly explains why medieval artists enjoyed drawing animals in general.
proves that the drawings were intended as jokes by the scribes who made them.
shows that the images were copied from a single lost manuscript.
inferences.e: The argument says the symbol’s distribution doesn’t match where that group mattered, so the proposal can’t explain all cases. Disproving one idea doesn’t prove jokes or a lost source.

inferences.p: In many languages, words for “mother” contain the sound m, a pattern that once led some linguists to propose a shared ancient origin. Others note that m is among the easiest sounds for infants to produce, since it requires only closing the lips while vocalizing, and that parents tend to interpret a baby’s earliest syllables as referring to them. If this second account is correct, then the similarity among these words ______
inferences.r: could have arisen independently in many languages rather than indicating a common ancestor.
w: must have spread from one language to another through trade.
shows that infants learn to speak earlier than linguists once believed.
would be expected only among languages that are closely related.
inferences.e: If infants’ physiology produces the pattern everywhere, no shared origin or borrowing is needed. Closely related languages wouldn’t be required.

inferences.p: When a large employer in one town offered free bus passes to its staff, car commuting there fell. Planners in a neighboring town copied the program but saw no change, even though its staff were offered the same passes. The first town, however, had frequent bus service throughout the day, whereas buses in the second town ran only twice each morning. Taken together, these facts suggest that ______
inferences.r: the cost of a bus trip may matter less to commuters than whether buses run often enough to be convenient.
w: workers in the second town were less concerned about the cost of commuting.
employers should not be expected to pay for their workers’ commuting costs.
free bus passes reduce car commuting wherever they are offered.
inferences.e: The same free passes worked only where service was frequent, so frequency appears to be what mattered. The second town’s result contradicts “wherever they are offered.”
